# Shown on Purpose {#sec-appearance}

A type that cannot show itself is a schema with no error messages. The
same instinct that wants a parser at the boundary wants a view at the
boundary. Structure, validity, and presentation are one design surface,
split into layers so they can change at different speeds.

R gets you part of the way by cultural habit. `print`, `format`, and
`str` are generics, so a class can own its appearance without owning the
console. [cli](https://cli.r-lib.org/) raised the ceiling: a package can
look like a small text interface, with semantic roles for alerts,
progress, and inline values, instead of a pile of pasted strings. You can
tell a finished package by the console. The unfinished ones dump
`print.default` and apologize with a vignette.

PowerShell gets you the rest of the idea, and then shows you how an idea
can outlive its file format.

## The pipe carries objects

Jeffrey Snover wrote the Monad manifesto on 8 August 2002. The public
copy lives on
[Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/scripting/developer/monad-manifesto)
and as a
[PDF](https://jsnover.com/Docs/MonadManifesto.pdf). The sentence that
matters, against a tradition of "prayer-based parsing" of text:

> Instead of piping unstructured text, we pipe .NET objects.

Downstream commands reflect on those objects. `Format-Table` is a command
at the end of the pipeline, not a conversion that happens in the middle.
The manifesto is explicit that once you have rendered text, you are back
in the world of prayer. Formatting is a host concern. The objects survive
until the host.

That is the alignment with the R taste, and it is worth saying without
irony. The substrate is a large, formally specified object runtime. The
experience on top is a shell: verbs, pipelines, streams, discoverable
help. The object model is the backbone. It is not the user interface.
R's version is less formal and strangely similar. SEXPs are the backbone.
Functions are the user interface. `print` is what the host does when the
pipeline ends and a human is watching.

## Format data is a view contract

`Format.ps1xml` files, and the views that replaced them, declare how a
type is shown: a table, a list, a wide view, a custom view. The official
description is
[about_Format.ps1xml](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_format.ps1xml).
The important sentence in that document: the formatting affects the
display only. It does not change which properties flow down the pipeline.

Beginning in PowerShell 6, the built-in views moved into the source code.
The XML files from Windows PowerShell 5.1 are not how the default views
are defined anymore. Custom `Format.ps1xml` files still work, and
`Update-FormatData` still loads them. The file format is the part that
aged. The separation did not. Wanting the idea "revamped into something
better" is in agreement with the direction the shell already took. Keep
the contract --- a declarative view, distinct from the value, swappable
by the host --- and retire the ceremony that got you there in 2006.

The Extended Type System is the companion move. ETS can adapt how a type
presents members and type names without you owning the class, which is
how a shell stays useful in a world of ADO tables, WMI objects, and XML
whose reflected shapes are not the shapes a human wants. The manifesto
calls the piece an extended type reflector. You do not subclass
`FileInfo` to make `Get-ChildItem` show `Length` and `LastWriteTime`.
You project it.

S3 generics are a cousin of that reflector. `format.my_class` adds a view
from outside the value. What R never grew is the declarative pack: a
data file, reviewed like data, that says "this class renders like so in
a console, and like so in a markdown table," without the rendering buried
in a method that mixes policy with string concatenation. cli themes and
format methods are the craft version. They work. They are code, so they
are harder to swap per host than a view definition would be. If you ever
build the missing piece, build it as data. The method can interpret the
data. The data should be the design.

## A short, unromantic history

The affection for this design sometimes gets told as a single arrow from
Cairo to Longhorn to WinFS to .NET to PowerShell. The arrow is a mood,
not a genealogy, and the mood survives a more accurate story.

COM gave Windows a binary notion of interface identity. `IUnknown`,
vtables, reference counts, a contract you could implement from more than
one language. It also gave the industry DLL hell. The idea that survived
is metadata and interfaces, not the binary layout.

Cairo was an early-1990s attempt at an object-oriented operating system.
It did not ship as conceived. Pieces of the thinking scattered into later
Windows. It is not the parent of the CLR.

Longhorn's WinFS was an attempt to make the filesystem a store of typed
items. It was cut. It did not grow up into .NET. The dream --- systems
that speak in typed items rather than opaque files --- is a recurring
Microsoft dream, and it has failed as a product more than once. The
failure does not make the dream stupid. It makes it a bad causal claim.

.NET is a managed runtime with serious metadata, designed around the turn
of the century, informed by COM's successes and scars and by other
language runtimes. PowerShell is Monad: Snover's bet that an
administrative shell on that runtime should pipe objects and format at
the edge. That bet shipped. It is the piece you can actually learn from,
because it has docs, an object pipeline, streams, and a view layer you
can point at.

Take the aesthetic and leave the arrow. Typed meaning in the middle.
Declarative projection at the host. Mutation and I/O quarantined. The
backbone can be SEXPs and generics, or CLR metadata and ETS. The shape of
the program is the part worth copying.

DSC, mentioned in the same breath, is the instinct aimed at desired state
instead of desired display: say what should be true, let the system
converge. It is a different feature and the same love of declarative
descriptions. This book does not have a chapter on configuration
management. It has a chapter on the love.

## What to do in an R package this week

You do not have format data. You have generics and cli. Use them as if
the view were a contract.

- Write `format.<class>` to return a character vector of the meaning, not
  a dump of the slots. One line if the value is a fact. A short block if
  the value is a document.
- Write `print.<class>` as a thin caller of `format`, returning the value
  invisibly, so the REPL stays a conversation.
- Use cli for situations: alerts, progress, inline code and values. Give
  the output semantic roles so a theme can restyle it.
- Keep the view free of decisions. Formatting does not fetch, validate,
  or mutate. If `print` has a side effect beyond writing, the contract is
  already confused.
- When a value has more than one useful projection --- a one-line summary,
  a verbose dump, a markdown row --- make those named functions, not
  flags buried in `print`. PowerShell's table-versus-list split is the
  model. You can ship it as `format` and `format_details` long before you
  have a view file format.

And connect it back to streams. The view is what success looks like. The
condition system is what the other channels look like. A package that
formats its values and signals its situations, and never `cat()`s either,
feels finished because both contracts are present. A package that only
computes the right answer still feels like a sketch. The console is part
of the product, especially in a language whose main instrument is a
conversation.
